District staff are beginning to plan the programming for the 2025 Summer School (Bulldog Summer Academy).

The plan is to host on-site Summer School for grades K-8 from June 4 to July 2 at Meadowmere Elementary and Martin City K8.  Students will enroll in the grade level they will enter in the fall.  Belvidere and Meadowmere students will attend Meadowmere Elementary.  Conn-West, Butcher-Greene, and Martin City students will attend Martin City K8.  Martin City 6-8 and Grandview Middle School students will attend Martin City K8.

High Grove students will attend at the High Grove Early Childhood Center.

Grandview High School will have in-person courses starting on June 4 and continuing until July 2. There will be a morning and afternoon session.  The virtual courses for credit attainment will begin on June 3 to June 28.  Virtual courses for credit recovery will be from July 8 to August 2.
Approve the summer school site locations and dates as presented.

Title: b. SIP Presentations - BV, BG, CW

fields.Content:
In response to the limited success of some research-based interventions in achieving widespread instructional improvements, educational researchers and practitioners have increasingly turned to the discipline of improvement science. In the book Learning to Improve: How America’s Schools Can Get Better at Getting Better, Anthony S. Bryk, Louis M. Gomez, Alicia Grunow, and Paul G. LeMahieu explore the application of improvement science in educational settings. Drawing from their work with the Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching, along with successful examples from other fields, they highlight the importance of adopting systematic approaches to drive meaningful change.

Utilizing the research of these Carnegie Foundation scholars and the six key principles of improvement science, we have applied these concepts in the development of our School Improvement Plan (SIP) format. The six key principles of improvement science are as follows:
  1. Make the work problem-specific and user-centered.
    It starts with a single question: “What specifically is the problem we are trying to solve?” It enlivens a co-development orientation: engage key participants early and often.
  2. Variation in performance is the core problem to address.
    The critical issue is not what works, but rather what works, for whom, and under what set of conditions. Aim to advance efficacy reliably at scale.
  3.  See the system that produces the current outcomes.
    It is hard to improve what you do not fully understand. Go and see how local conditions shape work processes. Make your hypotheses for change public and clear.
  4.  We cannot improve at scale what we cannot measure.
    Embed measures of key outcomes and processes to track if change is an improvement. We intervene in complex organizations. Anticipate unintended consequences and measure these too.
  5. Anchor practice improvement in disciplined inquiry.
    Engage rapid cycles of Plan, Do, Study, Act (PDSA) to learn fast, fail fast, and improve quickly. That failures may occur is not the problem; that we fail to learn from them is.
  6. Accelerate improvements through networked communities.
    Embrace the wisdom of crowds. We can accomplish more together than even the best of us can accomplish alone.
This approach also guides the work of our Building Leadership Teams (BLT) as they engage in the process of school improvement.

Three building principals will present updates on their School Improvement Plans (SIPs) based on their progress at this point in the school year. Presentations will be given by the principals, Dr. Samantha Dane - Belvidere Elementary, Dr. Kelly Nash - Butcher-Greene Elementary, and Ms. Bridget Williams - Conn-West Elementary.
Accept presentations as informational

The Board of Education recognizes the importance of parent/guardian, staff and student handbooks that accurately convey the policies, procedures and rules of the district to the individuals affected by them. The Board charges the administration with the responsibility for creating, revising, maintaining and disseminating such handbooks in accordance with Board policies and administrative procedures. 

The superintendent is charged with the responsibility for staff handbooks, and building principals are charged with responsibility for parent/guardian and student handbooks. The superintendent will approve all handbooks before publication, and all published handbooks will be made available to the Board per policy CHCA. 

As part of a continuous improvement process, Grandview High School revised their building’s tardy protocol (see page 127 of the Supporting Document).  This protocol has been edited within the parent/student handbook for review and has been approved by the Superintendent per Policy CHCA.  

The parent/student handbook will be uploaded in eBoardsolutions and will be accessible via the district website.

In August 2024, the Board approved a proposal from Strategos International (ATT 1) to address a School Resource Officer shortage in our schools. The board approved three School Protection Specialists (SPS) to be placed in three of our schools. All officers were highly trained and vetted through an extensive background check. District administration is recommending the addition of one officer (ATT 2) to also be stationed at the GHS but for use in all schools as needs arise. The term of the amended agreement will be for the remainder of the three-year agreement that started August 19, 2024.
Approve the amendment to the contract with Strategos International to provide an additional School Security Specialist for an amount of $67,417 in fiscal year 2025.

Policies.Name: Policy BF: SCHOOL BOARD POLICY PROCESS

fields.Content:
Each year the Board of Education sets the calendar for the following school year.  The goal has been to get the calendar set as soon as practical so that families and community can plan appropriately.  

Districts are required to provide 1044 hours of student attendance, with a minimum number of 169 student attendance days.  School calendars must also include 36 make-up hours for inclement weather, for a total of at least 1080 hours.  The proposed 2025-2026 calendar has 1084.5 student hours (165 full days and 4 half days) plus the 36 hours (6 days) for inclement weather or other emergencies.  This exceeds the number of state required hours in order to maintain approximately the same amount of student instructional time as the current and previous years.  Districts are required to start no sooner than 14 days prior to the first Monday in September. 

The proposed calendar is substantially similar to the 2024-25 calendar except that Spring Break starts on the 5th Monday rather than the 4th Monday to align with the Herndon Center calendar.The proposed calendar has 188 contracted days for teachers which includes five paid holidays and a flexed day for parent/teacher conferences, four additional days for new teachers' orientation, 169 days for student attendance and includes the additional built-in 36 hours for make-up days.

District Potpourri met several times this fall and sought feedback from employees at their sites.  Potpourri supports recommending the final proposed 2025-26 calendar and narrative, which can be found in Supporting Documents, to the Board of Education for approval.
Approve the calendar for school year 2025-2026 as presented in Supporting Documents.
